extracted.intended_audience: Canadian patent examiners, patent agents/attorneys and applicants (prosecuting or drafting Canadian patent applications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patentability issues in Canadian applications, specifically selection claims, provisos, utility (including demonstration and sound prediction), and new-matter/amendment limits. Intended to direct examiners and inform applicants on satisfying statutory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection — three conditions for patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The three conditions that must be satisfied for a patentable selection are that: the selection be based on some substantial advantage; the whole of the selection must possess the advantage; and the advantage must be in respect of a quality of a special character peculiar to the whole selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The advantage can include avoiding a substantial disadvantage; it must be in comparison to the overall group from which the selection has been made and be supported by sufficient representative testing rather than comparisons to a few isolated members. In assessing a selection, usual patentability requirements (novelty, utility, ingenuity/s inventive step, sufficiency of disclosure) must also be applied. A newly discovered, substantial advantage is necessary to provide the utility and inventive step for a selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage disclosure for selections
rubrics_metrics.description: The advantage underlying a selection must be properly disclosed; if unclear, the new utility arising from the advantage must also be disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no way to assess the purported 'advantage', a person skilled in the art cannot appreciate that an invention has been correctly and fully described. Mere statements that an embodiment is 'preferred' or possesses an unspecified advantage are not sufficient to disclose the substantial advantage necessary for inventive selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and anticipation for selections
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty of a selection rests on the fact that the selected aspects of the prior disclosure had not previously been made; if an operating embodiment within the selection claim has already been made, the claimed invention is anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If something within the selection claim was merely listed in a prior document without disclosing the advantage on which the selection is based, the requirement for prior disclosure is not met and there is no anticipation. Example: listing of generic 'buoyant bodies' does not anticipate a selection of tetrahedral bodies where prior art did not disclose that shape or its advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness assessment for selections (including obvious-to-try)
rubrics_metrics.description: A purported selection that is not anticipated may nevertheless be found obvious; assessment may consider whether the alleged advantage is truly unexpected and may involve an 'obvious to try' analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly in chemical arts, an obvious-to-try framework can be used to assess whether selection yields an inventive step; the unexpectedness of the advantage is a key factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisos to exclude prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A proviso is an exclusionary limitation introduced to a claim to exclude some specified matter (e.g. 'provided said attachment means is not a rubber-based adhesive'). A proviso based on prior art may be introduced to establish novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proviso should not introduce new matter (must comply with subsection 38.2 of the Patent Act). When introduced as an amendment, a proviso excluding a feature not necessarily present in the original claim should be carefully considered because the excluded feature is presumably not required for proper operation. A proviso can render a claim patentable where a broad claim would be novel/inventive if not for an isolated earlier disclosure. Multiple provisos require greater scrutiny to ensure remaining subject-matter is a single invention and the nature of the original invention is not obscured (e.g., defining what the invention is not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement (section 2 of the Patent Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be useful: it must be capable of an actual relevant use and not be fanciful, speculative, or inoperable. The usefulness must be related to the nature of the subject-matter as identified by claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Patent Act does not prescribe the degree of usefulness required; a single use related to the subject-matter suffices and the threshold is low ('a scintilla of utility will do'). Except where utility is the essence of the invention, the applicant need not expressly state the utility in the application, but if questioned, utility must have been demonstrated or soundly predicted as of the filing date. A claim must define the inventive element(s) necessary to enable proper operation; features understood by a person skilled in the art as implicit need not be explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controllability and reproducibility of utility
rubrics_metrics.description: To be considered useful an invention must be controllable and reliably reproducible; the desired result must inevitably follow when the invention is put into practice and not be left to chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An accepted degree of success or known production parameters in an art may suffice (e.g., recognized success ratio or acceptable reject rate). Inventions arrived at by chance or that cannot be reliably reproduced lack utility. Inventions that rely on subjective judgment in a way that introduces intuition, creativity or approximation may lack reproducibility and thus utility. Certain precise mental steps, however, do not of themselves cause lack of utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility must be established as of filing date (demonstration or sound prediction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility must be established as of the filing date either by demonstration or by sound prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an examiner has reasonable grounds to doubt utility and the applicant provides data, the data must show utility as of the filing date; the Commissioner must refuse if utility cannot be established by demonstration or sound prediction. Demonstration may be shown after filing by affidavit but must establish that demonstration existed as of filing. Demonstration should be by experimentation/testing of all embodiments or members of a claimed genus and cannot rely on bare assertions. Where demonstration is not possible, a sound prediction may be relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three components of a sound prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: A sound prediction analysis requires: (1) a factual basis for the prediction; (2) an articulable and 'sound' line of reasoning from which the desired result can be inferred from the factual basis; and (3) proper disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The factual basis generally comprises facts in the description and drawings, relevant scientific principles, and common general knowledge. The line of reasoning bridges the factual basis to the purported utility and must be understandable by a person skilled in the art. Proper disclosure requires that the description provide sufficient information such that a skilled person, in light of CGK, would understand the basis of the prediction and be able to predict the entire claimed scope would work when reduced to practice. The relevant date for soundness is the filing date; sound prediction is not a certainty but must be more than speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual basis specifics for sound prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: The factual basis may include experimental data but does not necessarily require it; it can be scientifically accepted laws/principles, data from the state of the art, or CGK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple unsubstantiated statements or prophetic examples are not factual. Sufficiency of factual basis depends on claim scope, state of the art, nature of invention, predictability, and how extensively the applicant explored the claimed area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound line of reasoning requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The sound line of reasoning must logically connect the factual basis to the purported utility in a manner that a person skilled in the art can understand how the desired result follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the line of reasoning is not articulable or is speculative, the prediction will be unsound. Where the line of reasoning depends on a theory necessary to show utility, that theory may need to be disclosed in the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper disclosure requirement for sound prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must disclose the factual basis and the sound line of reasoning sufficiently so that the skilled person could understand the basis of the prediction and predict that the entire scope of the claim would work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure must be present in the original description; evidence generated after filing cannot be used to supply the disclosure for sound prediction. Elements of the factual basis or reasoning that are CGK need not be repeated, but if the prediction relies on non-public information it must be included in the original description. The disclosure requirement for sound prediction is distinct from the sufficiency requirement under subsection 27(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples illustrating demonstration vs sound prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical examples demonstrate application of the rules: (1) where a specific polymer (calcium alginate) was demonstrated to work, and common general knowledge supported extrapolation to other polymers with the same structural features, a sound prediction supported a broader claim; (2) where only one specific gene mutation was shown to confer herbicide resistance and no basis existed to predict all domain mutations would do so, the broader claim failed utility for lack of sound prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples to assess whether factual basis, line of reasoning and disclosure exist across full claim scope. These examples illustrate when demonstration suffices and when sound prediction is required (and when it fails).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisos affecting utility (reassessment required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a proviso has been presented to avoid inoperative subject-matter, the basis upon which the utility of the remaining matter of the claim has been established must be reconsidered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since utility is often based on a sound prediction, excluding a known inoperative embodiment requires reassessing whether the line of reasoning that underpinned the utility still holds for the remaining claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office actions on utility — examiner reporting obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an examiner determines that utility is not established by demonstration or sound prediction, a defect will be identified under section 2 and the examiner must include supporting arguments detailing how the defect relates to the three-step sound prediction test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of inutility can arise at any time. An examiner may also present a separate and independent defect under subsection 27(3) (sufficiency of disclosure) if the description fails to enable the invention without undue experimentation or inventive skill; both defects should be separately identified with supporting arguments. Alleged inventions contrary to known scientific principles require demonstration of proper operation or will be identified as defective under section 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: New matter prohibition on amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Patent Act, the specification and drawings of an application may be amended provided the amendments do not contain new matter compared to what was filed originally (subsection 38.2(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matter pertaining to prior art may be added only if acknowledged as prior art. Amendments that remove matter may also cause non-compliance if the removal results in descriptions outside what was reasonably inferable from the original filing. If an examiner finds new matter in an amendment, a defect will be identified and the applicant must remove the new matter. Amendments containing new matter will be laid open and may affect the applicant's later ability to obtain patents in Canada or elsewhere for inventions relying on the new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment requirements for applications originally filed in another language (regular Canadian non‑PCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to regularly-filed Canadian (non-PCT) applications originally filed in a language other than English or French must be reasonable to infer from both: (1) the specification and drawings as filed on the filing date; and (2) the specification or drawings immediately after replacement by an English or French translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translated documents submitted under the Patent Rules replace the originally filed specification and drawings; examination for new matter proceeds on the basis of the translated documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment limits for PCT national phase applications filed in another language
rubrics_metrics.description: PCT national phase applications originally filed in a language other than English or French are governed by Patent Rules subsection 155.6(1) rather than subsection 38.2(3); amendments after entering national phase must be reasonable to infer from both the international application's specification/drawings on its filing date and the translated text matter submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments cannot be based on untranslated text matter unless (a) the amendments are reasonable to infer from the remainder of the specification/drawings (excluding untranslated terms), or (b) the untranslated terms are present in non-language-dependent free text in a sequence listing. If English/French text appears in the sequence listing, that may affect amendment permissibility.
